newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan bankers see forex crunch in June.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan bankers see forex crunch in June.

text.p: Pakistan is likely to face a severe foreign exchange crunch in June when debt payments estimated at $925 million fall due, bankers said on Wednesday.

They said last week's decision by the State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP) to allow banks to roll over three-month forex deposits brought in from abroad and placed with the SBP could add about $350 million to scheduled repayments of $575 million.

"This shows Pakistan is desperate and despite claims that the new government has raised investor confidence, Pakistan's borrowing cost has remained unchanged," Maqsood Ahmed, vice-president of Muslim Commercial Bank, told Reuters.
"It will be difficult for Pakistan to tide over such a massive repayment in June," he said, adding that the government might have to roll over the deposits for another three months.

A central bank official confirmed the SBP had asked banks to roll over the high-yielding forex deposits they had placed in a special central bank account under a scheme launched on October 22 to bolster Pakistan's sagging reserves.
The official, who asked not to be named, declined to comment on the impact of the move or to specify June debt payments.
The scheme offered banks a 17 percent annual return on the rupee equivalent of sums deposited with the SBP. Bankers say the return is equivalent to about 12 percent in dollar terms.

The scheme, part of a "mini-budget" unveiled by the ousted government led by Benazir Bhutto on October 22, was harshly criticised as too expensive by Nawaz Sharif's Pakistan Muslim League party, then in opposition and now ruling the country.
Bankers said most of the deposits were brought in only a few days before expiry of the scheme's December 10 deadline.
The research head of a foreign investment bank, who asked not to be named, said the scheme had attracted about $450 million, of which some $350 million might be rolled over.
"Debt repayments falling in June were estimated at $575 million. If $350 million is rolled over for another three months as expected, repayments in June come to $925 million," he said.
Pakistan's foreign reserves, excluding bullion, stood at $1.0 billion on March 1, compared to $1.33 billion a year ago.
Sharif, who swept to victory in February 3 polls, has vowed to tackle Pakistan's $30 billion foreign debt as a top priority.
Last month he announced a National Debt Retirement Scheme, asking Pakistanis at home and abroad to send cash, interest-free loans and deposits in foreign currency to pay off the debt.
Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz told bankers this week the scheme had raised $55 million with $175 million more committed.
Bankers said the rollover offer showed Pakistan was still scrambling to meet March debt payments of around $600 million.
"For most banks it is not a bad deal as premiums on forward dollars have dropped drastically during the past few weeks amid low demand from importers," Ahmed said.
The premium on six-month forward dollars has slipped to six percent from a peak of 10 percent about two months ago.
